title: Visiting Medina
hook: many visit the Prophet's Mosque, though it isn't part of Hajj

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell tawaf, and your line: goodbye to the house. When you left somewhere today, did you turn and say goodbye on purpose? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

Don't saddle up for a journey, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, except to three mosques. That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it. The Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Messenger's own mosque in Medina, and the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. The Hajj is over, and its rites are finished in Mecca. But some pilgrims, before the pilgrimage or after it, take the road north to the city where he lived, prayed and is buried. Today, visiting Medina.
screen: `ONLY THREE MOSQUES.` → `THE MESSENGER'S MOSQUE.` → `THE ROAD NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, what it isn't. Visiting Medina isn't part of Hajj. A pilgrim who goes straight home from Mecca has a complete Hajj. The visit is its own act, often joined to the trip because the road is already long. Second, what the mosque is. In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet says a prayer in this mosque of his is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except the Sacred Mosque. And he says that between his house and his pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise. Visitors try to pray in that small stretch, the Rawdah, the garden. Third, the greeting. His grave is there, in what was once Aisha's room. Visitors stand near it and say, as-salamu alayka ya rasul Allah: peace be on you, messenger of God. In Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet says that no one greets him but that God returns his soul to him so that he returns the greeting. Scholars have discussed how to frame the journey. Some say the traveler should set out for the mosque, and greet the Prophet once there, holding to the report about three mosques. Others hold the visit to the grave itself to be a recommended act. Both send peace on him. Fourth, the line under all of it. Surah Al-Ahzab says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Muslims call that sending salawat, and it isn't tied to Medina. It can be said anywhere, in a kitchen, on a bus, inside the daily prayer. The visitors in Medina say it standing a few steps from him. Everyone else says it from wherever they are.
screen: `NOT PART OF HAJJ.` · `A GARDEN BETWEEN HOUSE AND PULPIT.` · `HE RETURNS THE GREETING.` · `SEND BLESSINGS FROM ANYWHERE.` · then, large: `PEACE BE ON YOU, MESSENGER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: The practice: send salawat. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say, slowly, as-salamu alayka ayyuha an-nabiyy, peace be on you, O Prophet, the words from the tashahhud in the prayer. Or say sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, a few times, unhurried. If you don't, think of a teacher whose words still reach you, and send them, in your mind, a plain thank you. Then sit, and let the greeting settle. The bell holds the time.
Visiting Medina. A journey to the Prophet's Mosque and a greeting of peace at his grave, made by some pilgrims, but not part of the Hajj. Today's word.

Your line: peace on you, messenger. Today, when the Prophet's name comes up, in a lesson, a conversation or a thought, pause and send peace on him. Tomorrow: the Hajj of the heart. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1139 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HAJJ OF THE HEART.`

howItsDone: Some pilgrims travel to Medina before or after Hajj to pray in the Prophet's Mosque and greet him at his grave; Muslims send salawat on him in prayer and when his name is mentioned.

fork.setup: you want to set out on a journey for the sake of worship in a mosque. by the report in Bukhari, which mosques are worth saddling up for?
options: the Sacred Mosque, the Aqsa Mosque, and the Prophet's mosque.
fork.reveal: the Prophet named three: the Sacred Mosque, the Messenger's mosque, and the Aqsa Mosque.

original.note: peace be on you, said to one person: the greeting visitors give the Prophet.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last stop of the Hajj.
what it means: a separate visit to the Prophet's Mosque and a greeting of peace at his grave.
what a scholar hears: the report of the three mosques, and a long discussion of how to frame the journey.

sources.quoted: Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation.

notes: Bukhari 1189 (three mosques), 1190 (a prayer in this mosque better than a thousand elsewhere except al-Masjid al-Haram), 1196 (between my house and my pulpit, a garden of Paradise). Confirm numbers.
Abu Dawud 2041 (God returns his soul so he returns the greeting): confirm number and grading.
Pickthall 33:56 wording: verify exactly before release.

The scholarly difference over setting out to visit the grave (e.g. Ibn Taymiyyah's view vs. scholars who hold ziyarah recommended) is given without naming or ranking; a Keeper should check the framing is fair to both sides and suitable for the path.
'The grave... in what was once Aisha's room' and 'visitors try to pray in the Rawdah' are general descriptions not in the cited texts; confirm.
The outline says 'many visit'; the script says 'some pilgrims' to keep to the claims rule.
Practice invites the tashahhud greeting and salawat 'if you pray' (real, existing words); no new prayer written.

Editor: Bukhari 1189's wording names 'the mosque of the Messenger' (the 'this mosque of mine' phrasing belongs to Abu Sa'id's report, Bukhari 1197), so hook, screen and fork now follow 1189's names and order; 'beside the mosque' changed to 'there', since the room now lies within the enlarged mosque.
